Generate three learning HTML files for the concept "Graceful native-extension fallback in a Python GUI". This is for a HFT trading practice repo.

Context:
- src/oil_alpha/oil_volume.py: wrapper that tries `import oil_volume_cpp` and sets USING_CPP=True/False
- app/dashboard.py: checks USING_CPP and shows "running unoptimised" warning when False
- The fallback uses pure Python implementations of the same functions (capacity_utilization, days_of_supply, fill_rate, rolling_mean)
- The pattern: try/except ImportError at module import time → flag → conditional dispatch

Please create:

1. /home/node/work/normal_work/HFT_Trading_Practice_Repo/docs/learning/lessons/0003-native-extension-fallback.html
   Concepts: ImportError guard at module level, USING_CPP sentinel flag, conditional dispatch, why the fallback must be a thin mirror (not a parallel feature set), dashboard UX for capability flags, math.isnan for NaN handling in pure Python, why the identical function signatures matter

2. /home/node/work/normal_work/HFT_Trading_Practice_Repo/docs/learning/drills/0003-native-extension-fallback.html
   8+ MCQ with feedback, 3 written recall questions with answers

3. /home/node/work/normal_work/HFT_Trading_Practice_Repo/docs/learning/vocab/0003-native-extension-fallback.html
   Terms: ImportError guard, USING_CPP flag, capability flag, thin fallback, conditional dispatch, native extension, pure Python fallback, graceful degradation, NaN (Python), st.warning

All files: self-contained with inline CSS. No external deps.

Also update /home/node/work/normal_work/HFT_Trading_Practice_Repo/docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md and PROGRESS.md.

"""Streamlit dashboard for the CL-vs-XLE lead-lag study.

Run:  ``streamlit run app/dashboard.py``

Shows live pipeline *progress*, a *results* panel (CCF curve, Granger p-values,
cointegration verdict, rolling corr/beta), and a *costs* panel with the three
flavours the user asked for: API free-tier budget, hypothetical transaction
cost, and per-stage compute time.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import sys

# Make ``src`` importable when run via ``streamlit run app/dashboard.py``.
_SRC = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "..", "src")
if _SRC not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath(_SRC))

import pandas as pd  # noqa: E402
import plotly.graph_objects as go  # noqa: E402
import streamlit as st  # noqa: E402

from oil_alpha.config import DEFAULT_START, LAG, LEAD, SYMBOLS, RunConfig, default_end  # noqa: E402
from oil_alpha.pipeline import ProgressEvent, run_pipeline  # noqa: E402

st.set_page_config(page_title="Crude-Oil Lead-Lag Lab", layout="wide")
st.title("🛢️ Crude-Oil Lead-Lag Lab")
st.caption(
    f"Does **{SYMBOLS[LEAD]} (WTI futures)** lead **{SYMBOLS[LAG]} (energy ETF)**? "
    "Daily study per the crude-oil research paper, Stages 1-3."
)

# --- Sidebar: run controls ---------------------------------------------------
with st.sidebar:
    st.header("Run settings")
    start = st.text_input("Start date", DEFAULT_START)
    end = st.text_input("End date", default_end())
    return_kind = st.radio("Return type", ["log", "simple"], horizontal=True)
    max_lag = st.slider("Max lag (trading days)", 1, 30, 10)
    rolling_window = st.slider("Rolling window", 20, 120, 60, step=10)
    drop_roll_days = st.checkbox("Drop CL=F roll-day jumps", value=True)
    use_cache = st.checkbox("Use local cache", value=True)
    turnover = st.number_input("Hypothetical turnover / yr", 1.0, 1000.0, 252.0, step=10.0)
    run = st.button("▶ Run pipeline", type="primary", use_container_width=True)
    st.markdown(
        "<small>yfinance + FRED need no API key. Negative-price (Apr-2020) and "
        "roll-day traps are handled automatically.</small>",
        unsafe_allow_html=True,
    )


def _ccf_figure(ll) -> go.Figure:
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_bar(x=ll.lags, y=ll.ccf, name="CCF")
    fig.add_vline(x=ll.peak_lag, line_dash="dash", line_color="crimson")
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=ll.peak_lag, y=ll.peak_corr,
        text=f"peak lag {ll.peak_lag}", showarrow=True, arrowhead=2,
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Cross-correlation  ρ(k)=corr({ll.x_name}ₜ, {ll.y_name}ₜ₊ₖ)   (k>0 ⇒ {ll.x_name} leads)",
        xaxis_title="lag k (days)", yaxis_title="correlation", height=340,
        margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=50, b=10),
    )
    return fig


def _line(series: pd.Series, title: str, yaxis: str) -> go.Figure:
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_scatter(x=series.index, y=series.to_numpy(), mode="lines")
    fig.update_layout(title=title, yaxis_title=yaxis, height=300, margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=40, b=10))
    return fig


def _render_results(result) -> None:
    ll = result.leadlag
    st.subheader("Results")

    c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
    leader = "CL (futures)" if ll.x_leads else ("XLE" if ll.peak_lag < 0 else "contemporaneous")
    c1.metric("Lead-lag leader", leader, f"peak lag {ll.peak_lag}")
    if result.granger:
        g = result.granger["x->y"]
        c2.metric(f"Granger {SYMBOLS[LEAD]}→{SYMBOLS[LAG]}", f"p={g.p_value:.3f}",
                  "significant" if g.significant else "n.s.")
    if result.spot_check:
        c3.metric("CL=F vs FRED spot", f"{result.spot_check['median_abs_pct']:.1f}%",
                  f"{result.spot_check['common_days']} common days")

    st.plotly_chart(_ccf_figure(ll), use_container_width=True)

    gc, cc = st.columns(2)
    with gc:
        st.markdown("**Granger causality (both directions)**")
        if result.granger:
            rows = [
                {"direction": g.direction, "best lag": g.best_lag,
                 "p-value": round(g.p_value, 4), "significant": g.significant}
                for g in result.granger.values()
            ]
            st.dataframe(pd.DataFrame(rows), hide_index=True, use_container_width=True)
            st.caption("Granger = predictive precedence, not true causation (paper Part 2.3).")
    with cc:
        st.markdown("**Cointegration (price levels)**")
        if result.eg_coint:
            st.write("•", result.eg_coint.verdict)
        if result.johansen_coint:
            st.write("•", result.johansen_coint.verdict)

    rc, rb = st.columns(2)
    if result.rolling_corr is not None and not result.rolling_corr.empty:
        rc.plotly_chart(
            _line(result.rolling_corr, f"Rolling correlation ({SYMBOLS[LEAD]} vs {SYMBOLS[LAG]})", "corr"),
            use_container_width=True,
        )
    if result.rolling_beta is not None and not result.rolling_beta.empty:
        rb.plotly_chart(
            _line(result.rolling_beta, f"Rolling β of {SYMBOLS[LAG]} to oil", "beta"),
            use_container_width=True,
        )

    if result.warnings:
        for w in result.warnings:
            st.warning(w)


def _render_costs(result) -> None:
    st.subheader("Projected costs")
    a, b, c = st.tabs(["① API free-tier budget", "② Transaction cost", "③ Compute / time"])

    with a:
        rows = result.budget.as_rows()
        if rows:
            df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
            st.dataframe(df, hide_index=True, use_container_width=True)
            for r in rows:
                if r["cap"] is not None:
                    st.progress(min(1.0, r["fraction"] or 0.0),
                                text=f"{r['source']}: {r['used']}/{r['cap']} used")
        st.caption(f"Total requests this run: {result.budget.total_requests()} "
                   "(yfinance/FRED have no hard cap; capped sources shown with bars).")

    with b:
        if result.cost_estimates:
            df = pd.DataFrame([
                {"asset": SYMBOLS.get(c.asset_key, c.asset_key),
                 "round-trip (bp)": round(c.round_trip_bp, 2),
                 "turnover/yr": c.turnover_per_year,
                 "annual drag (bp)": round(c.annual_drag_bp, 1),
                 "annual drag (%)": round(c.annual_drag_pct, 2)}
                for c in result.cost_estimates
            ])
            st.dataframe(df, hide_index=True, use_container_width=True)
        st.caption("Illustrative half-spread + commission assumptions (config.COST_MODEL), "
                   "not calibrated to live quotes.")

    with c:
        if result.metrics:
            st.dataframe(pd.DataFrame(result.metrics.as_rows()), hide_index=True, use_container_width=True)
            st.metric("Total compute time", f"{result.metrics.total_seconds:.2f} s")


def _run(cfg: RunConfig) -> None:
    progress = st.progress(0.0, text="starting…")
    with st.status("Running pipeline…", expanded=True) as status:
        final = None
        for event in run_pipeline(cfg):
            progress.progress(event.pct, text=f"{event.stage} — {event.message}")
            icon = {"ok": "✅", "warn": "⚠️", "error": "❌", "done": "🏁"}.get(event.status, "•")
            if event.status != "start":
                st.write(f"{icon} **{event.stage}** — {event.message}")
            if event.stage == "done":
                final = event.payload
        status.update(label="Pipeline complete", state="complete")
    st.session_state["result"] = final


if run:
    cfg = RunConfig(
        start=start, end=end, return_kind=return_kind, max_lag=max_lag,
        rolling_window=rolling_window, drop_roll_days=drop_roll_days,
        use_cache=use_cache, turnover_per_year=turnover,
    )
    _run(cfg)

result = st.session_state.get("result")
if result is not None and result.leadlag is not None:
    _render_results(result)
    st.divider()
    _render_costs(result)
elif result is not None:
    st.error("Pipeline aborted before producing results. Check warnings above / network access.")
else:
    st.info("Set your window in the sidebar and click **▶ Run pipeline** to begin.")

1	# Glossary
2	
3	Terms introduced across all learning modules in this repo. Each term links to the vocab file where it is defined in full.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 0001 — pybind11 + CMake FetchContent
8	
9	Source: [vocab/0001-pybind11-cmake-extension.html](vocab/0001-pybind11-cmake-extension.html)
10	
11	| Term | Type | One-line definition |
12	|------|------|---------------------|
13	| **pybind11** | Library | Header-only C++ library that exposes C++ types and functions to Python via compile-time template metaprogramming — no code generation step. |
14	| **PYBIND11_MODULE** | C++ Macro | Generates the `extern "C" PyObject* PyInit_<name>()` entry point that Python's import machinery calls after `dlopen()`-ing the shared library. |
15	| **pybind11_add_module** | CMake Function | CMake wrapper around `add_library(SHARED)` that sets the correct Python extension suffix, strips the `lib` prefix, applies `-fvisibility=hidden`, and enables LTO in Release mode. |
16	| **FetchContent** | CMake Module | Downloads external CMake dependencies at configure time and makes their targets available in the same CMake scope. Used as a fallback when pybind11 is not pip-installed. |
17	| **scikit-build-core** | Build Backend | PEP 517 build backend that invokes CMake when pip builds a wheel, enabling `pip install .` to compile C++ extensions automatically. |
18	| **PYBIND11_FINDPYTHON** | CMake Variable | When set to `ON` before `find_package(pybind11)`, instructs pybind11 to use CMake's modern `FindPython3` module instead of the deprecated `FindPythonLibs` — essential for venv and uv-managed Pythons. |
19	| **editable install** | Python Packaging | `pip install -e .` mode where Python source changes are immediately importable; C++ extension changes still require a recompile. |
20	| **ABI** | Concept | Application Binary Interface — the compiled-code contract. Python C extensions are ABI-tagged (e.g. `cpython-312`) and are not binary-compatible across Python versions. |
21	| **shared object (.so)** | OS Concept | Native library loaded at runtime via `dlopen()`. A Python C extension is a `.so` with a `PyInit_` entry point. On macOS it is `.dylib`; on Windows, `.pyd`. |
22	| **parity test** | Testing Pattern | Verifies a C++ implementation produces the same output as a NumPy reference within floating-point tolerance (e.g. `1e-9`). Serves as both a correctness gate and a regression guard. |
23	| **type caster** | pybind11 Concept | Compile-time template specialisation that converts C++ types to Python objects and back at the function call boundary (e.g. `std::vector<double>` ↔ `list[float]` via `pybind11/stl.h`). |

"""Crude-oil lead-lag quant research starter kit.

Grounded in ``crude_oil_research.txt`` Parts 1-2 (data sources + lead-lag
methodology) and the Stage 1-3 recommendations.
"""

__version__ = "0.1.0"
"""Cleaning that respects the paper's known traps (Part 2.1 + Caveats).

Three hazards are handled explicitly:

1. **Negative prices break log returns.** On 2020-04-20 the NYMEX WTI May
   contract settled at -$37.63/bbl, so ``ln(P_t / P_{t-1})`` is undefined across
   that window. :func:`to_returns` refuses to take logs of non-positive prices
   and points the caller at the offending dates.
2. **CL=F is a rolled continuous series.** Front-month roll dates inject jumps
   that are not real returns; :func:`flag_roll_days` detects them and they can be
   dropped.
3. **Alignment.** Returns are computed per column then inner-joined on common
   dates so the lead-lag estimators see a synchronous frame with no NaN/inf.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from oil_alpha.config import NEGATIVE_PRICE_WINDOW


class NegativePriceError(ValueError):
    """Raised when log returns are requested over a series that crosses <= 0."""


def to_returns(prices: pd.Series, kind: str = "log") -> pd.Series:
    """Daily returns for one price series.

    ``kind="log"`` requires strictly positive prices and raises
    :class:`NegativePriceError` otherwise (the Apr-2020 trap). ``kind="simple"``
    is defined wherever the *previous* price is non-zero and is the recommended
    fallback across the negative-price window.
    """
    prices = prices.dropna()
    if kind == "log":
        nonpos = prices[prices <= 0]
        if not nonpos.empty:
            first = nonpos.index[0].date()
            raise NegativePriceError(
                f"log returns undefined: '{prices.name}' has non-positive prices "
                f"(first at {first}). Use kind='simple' or a positive proxy "
                f"(USO / FRED DCOILWTICO) across {NEGATIVE_PRICE_WINDOW}."
            )
        out = np.log(prices / prices.shift(1))
    elif kind == "simple":
        out = prices / prices.shift(1) - 1.0
        out = out.replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown return kind: {kind!r} (use 'log' or 'simple')")
    return out.dropna().rename(prices.name)


def has_negative_prices(prices: pd.Series) -> bool:
    return bool((prices.dropna() <= 0).any())


def flag_roll_days(
    prices: pd.Series, threshold: float = 0.10, window: tuple[str, str] | None = None
) -> pd.Series:
    """Boolean mask of suspected front-month roll-day discontinuities in CL=F.

    A roll shows up as an outsized one-day jump that is a contract switch, not a
    real return. We flag |simple return| > ``threshold`` (default 10%). The
    Apr-2020 window is itself an expiry artifact, so days inside ``window`` (if
    given) are always flagged.
    """
    simple = prices.dropna()
    simple = (simple / simple.shift(1) - 1.0).replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    mask = simple.abs() > threshold
    mask = mask.fillna(False)
    if window is not None:
        lo, hi = pd.Timestamp(window[0]), pd.Timestamp(window[1])
        in_window = (prices.index >= lo) & (prices.index <= hi)
        mask = mask | pd.Series(in_window, index=prices.index)
    return mask.rename(f"{prices.name}_roll_flag")


def build_returns_frame(
    prices: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    kind: str = "log",
    drop_roll_days: bool = True,
    roll_col: str | None = "wti_fut",
    roll_threshold: float = 0.10,
) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
    """Turn a multi-column price frame into an aligned return frame + flags.

    Returns ``(returns, flags)`` where ``returns`` is inner-joined on common
    dates with no NaN/inf, and ``flags`` records per-date booleans (e.g. roll
    days, negative-window) for transparency on the dashboard.

    If ``kind="log"`` but a column crosses <= 0 (CL=F over Apr-2020), that single
    column automatically falls back to simple returns and is flagged, rather than
    failing the whole run -- the paper's recommended handling (b).
    """
    ret_cols: dict[str, pd.Series] = {}
    fallback_cols: list[str] = []
    for col in prices.columns:
        series = prices[col]
        if kind == "log" and has_negative_prices(series):
            ret_cols[col] = to_returns(series, kind="simple")
            fallback_cols.append(col)
        else:
            ret_cols[col] = to_returns(series, kind=kind)

    returns = pd.concat(ret_cols.values(), axis=1, join="inner").dropna()

    flags = pd.DataFrame(index=returns.index)
    lo, hi = pd.Timestamp(NEGATIVE_PRICE_WINDOW[0]), pd.Timestamp(NEGATIVE_PRICE_WINDOW[1])
    flags["negative_window"] = (returns.index >= lo) & (returns.index <= hi)

    if roll_col is not None and roll_col in prices.columns:
        roll_mask = flag_roll_days(
            prices[roll_col], threshold=roll_threshold, window=NEGATIVE_PRICE_WINDOW
        ).reindex(returns.index, fill_value=False)
        flags["roll_day"] = roll_mask.to_numpy()
        if drop_roll_days:
            returns = returns[~flags["roll_day"].to_numpy()]
            flags = flags.loc[returns.index]

    flags["log_fallback_to_simple"] = bool(fallback_cols)
    return returns, flags

(Part 1, bottom line): yfinance for CL=F/XLE/USO/XOM/CVX cross-checked against

"""

Lesson 0003  /  HFT Trading Practice Repo

Graceful Native-Extension Fallback
in a Python GUI

How oil_volume.py wraps oil_volume_cpp with an ImportError guard, a USING_CPP sentinel, and a thin pure-Python mirror — and how the Streamlit dashboard surfaces that capability flag to the user.

Contents

  1. The problem: optional native extension
  2. The ImportError guard at module level
  3. The USING_CPP sentinel flag
  4. Conditional dispatch: one public API, two backends
  5. Why the fallback must be a thin mirror
  6. Why identical function signatures matter
  7. math.isnan for NaN handling in pure Python
  8. Dashboard UX: surfacing capability flags with st.warning
  9. End-to-end mental model

1. The Problem: Optional Native Extension

The oil_volume_cpp shared library (.so) is produced by a CMake build step. It delivers fast C++ implementations of the oil-volume metric kernels. But a shared library can be absent for several legitimate reasons:

  • A fresh clone before the developer has run pip install -e . or ./scripts/build_cpp.sh
  • A CI runner that does not have a C++ toolchain available
  • A deployment target (e.g. Streamlit Community Cloud) where the wheel cannot be built
  • A Python version mismatch — the existing .so has the wrong ABI tag

The system must not crash in any of these situations. The goal is graceful degradation: continue running with correct (but slower) pure-Python implementations, and make the capability gap visible to the user rather than silently hiding it.

This repo's case oil_volume.py in src/oil_alpha/ is the wrapper module. It exposes four public functions — capacity_utilization, days_of_supply, fill_rate, and rolling_mean — that always work, regardless of whether the C++ extension was compiled. The dashboard at app/dashboard.py imports from this wrapper, never from oil_volume_cpp directly.

2. The ImportError Guard at Module Level

The guard is placed at the very top of oil_volume.py, before any function definitions. Python executes module-level code exactly once when the module is first imported. The try/except ImportError pattern attempts the native import and silently falls through on failure:

src/oil_alpha/oil_volume.py
try:
    import oil_volume_cpp as _cpp
    USING_CPP = True
except ImportError:
    USING_CPP = False
    _cpp = None  # keeps type checkers happy; never dereferenced when USING_CPP is False

Why at module level, not inside each function

Placing the import inside each function would re-attempt the import on every call — expensive when the extension is missing, and wrong semantically. Module-level placement means the import is tried once, the result is cached in USING_CPP, and every subsequent function call reads a boolean. This is the standard Python idiom for optional heavy imports.

Why catch only ImportError

Only ImportError (and its subclass ModuleNotFoundError) should be caught here. If the .so file exists but contains a bug that raises RuntimeError or ValueError at import time, that is a real error that should propagate. Catching too broadly would mask genuine bugs in the extension's module-level initialisation code.

Do not catch Exception or BaseException here except Exception would silently swallow initialisation bugs, segfault-on-load errors, and dependency failures inside the extension. Only ImportError corresponds to "the extension is not installed or not loadable" — which is the legitimate degradation scenario.

3. The USING_CPP Sentinel Flag

The boolean USING_CPP is the module's capability flag. It is set once at import time and is never mutated afterwards. Its value is readable by any code that imports oil_volume:

from oil_alpha import oil_volume
print(oil_volume.USING_CPP)  # True or False

This lets other modules — especially the dashboard — make branching decisions based on what backend is active, without those modules needing to know anything about oil_volume_cpp directly.

Naming convention

The name USING_CPP follows Python's convention of uppercase for module-level constants. The name should be positive and specific: it describes what is active, not what is missing. A name like CPP_UNAVAILABLE works but requires negation everywhere it is tested; USING_CPP reads naturally as a condition: if USING_CPP: ....

Thread safety

Since USING_CPP is set once at import time and never mutated, it is safe to read from multiple threads without locking. Python's GIL protects the single write; all subsequent reads are safe because the value never changes.

One flag for the whole session The capability flag captures a system property (is the extension compiled and loadable?) that does not change during a session. There is no need to re-check it per-call. The module-level boolean is the lightest possible mechanism.

4. Conditional Dispatch: One Public API, Two Backends

Each public function in oil_volume.py tests USING_CPP and routes to either the C++ implementation or the pure-Python fallback. The caller sees a single function signature regardless of backend:

src/oil_alpha/oil_volume.py
def rolling_mean(values: list[float], window: int) -> list[float]:
    """Compute a rolling arithmetic mean. Uses C++ kernel when available."""
    if USING_CPP:
        return _cpp.rolling_mean(values, window)
    return _py_rolling_mean(values, window)


def capacity_utilization(volume: float, capacity: float) -> float:
    """Capacity utilization ratio [0, 1]. Uses C++ kernel when available."""
    if USING_CPP:
        return _cpp.capacity_utilization(volume, capacity)
    return _py_capacity_utilization(volume, capacity)


# … days_of_supply and fill_rate follow the same pattern

The dispatch if USING_CPP is a simple boolean check — essentially free. It is not a try/except around the C++ call; the capability was already determined at import time. This means there is no per-call overhead from exception handling, and no possibility of the C++ call silently failing at runtime without the pure-Python branch catching it (a dangerous anti-pattern).

oil_volume.rolling_mean(values, window) │ if USING_CPP? ┌─────────┴──────────┐ Yes No │ │ _cpp.rolling_mean() _py_rolling_mean() (C++ shared library) (pure Python loop) │ │ └─────────┬──────────┘ same list[float] return value

5. Why the Fallback Must Be a Thin Mirror

The pure-Python functions in oil_volume.py must be thin mirrors of their C++ counterparts — identical semantics, same inputs, same outputs, same edge-case behaviour. They must not add features, change behaviour on edge inputs, or introduce new parameters.

The parallel-feature-set anti-pattern

If the Python fallback adds extra logging, different NaN handling, or additional validation that the C++ version does not have, then the two backends have different semantics. Code that passes tests with the C++ backend may fail silently with the Python backend, or vice versa. The fallback ceases to be a fallback and becomes a different implementation — one you must maintain in sync indefinitely.

Anti-pattern: divergent fallback If the Python fallback raises ValueError on negative capacity but the C++ version returns 0.0, then behaviour differs by backend. A test suite that always runs with C++ present will not catch the Python path. When a deployment environment loses C++, the dashboard breaks in production.

The thin mirror rule

Write the pure-Python implementation first. Verify it gives the same output as the C++ version across all inputs including edge cases (zero, negative, NaN, empty list). Then make the C++ implementation match that spec, not the other way around. The Python version is the reference; C++ is the optimisation.

How to verify parity The parity test pattern from Lesson 0001 applies here: compare each pure-Python function against its C++ counterpart across a representative input set, asserting equality within tolerance. This is a required test — it is not optional because the fallback only runs when C++ is absent, which is exactly when tests might not be running either.

6. Why Identical Function Signatures Matter

Both backends — C++ and pure Python — must expose exactly the same function signature: same parameter names, same types, same positional order, same default values, same return type. This is what makes the dispatch transparent to callers.

# C++ side (pybind11 binding, from cpp/oil_volume/bindings.cpp):
m.def("rolling_mean", &rolling_mean,
     py::arg("values"), py::arg("window"));

# Python fallback (oil_volume.py):
def _py_rolling_mean(values: list[float], window: int) -> list[float]: ...

# Public wrapper — same signature as both backends:
def rolling_mean(values: list[float], window: int) -> list[float]: ...

What breaks when signatures diverge

DivergenceEffect
Python fallback adds a validate=True parameterCode that passes validate=False fails with TypeError when C++ is active (it doesn't accept validate)
C++ uses positional-only, Python requires keywordCallers writing rolling_mean(values=x, window=3) fail with C++ backend
C++ returns list[float], Python returns a generatorCode that calls len() on the result breaks on Python backend
C++ returns NaN for warm-up, Python returns NoneDownstream float arithmetic crashes on Python backend

Identical signatures also make the wrapper function trivial: it is just a conditional redirect. There is no signature translation, no argument remapping, no output conversion — those would all be signs that the two backends are not truly equivalent.

7. math.isnan for NaN Handling in Pure Python

Both the C++ and Python implementations of rolling_mean emit float('nan') for the warm-up period (the first window - 1 positions where not enough values have been seen). The pure-Python fallback must produce this in exactly the same positions.

src/oil_alpha/oil_volume.py — pure Python rolling_mean
import math

def _py_rolling_mean(values: list[float], window: int) -> list[float]:
    if window <= 0:
        raise ValueError("window must be positive")
    n = len(values)
    out = [float("nan")] * n        # pre-fill with NaN (warm-up positions)
    running_sum = 0.0
    for i in range(n):
        running_sum += values[i]
        if i >= window:
            running_sum -= values[i - window]
        if i + 1 >= window:
            out[i] = running_sum / window
    return out

Why math.isnan and not == float('nan')

NaN is the only value in IEEE 754 floating-point that is not equal to itself. float('nan') == float('nan') is False. To test whether a float is NaN in pure Python, you must use math.isnan(x) (or equivalently x != x, but that is unreadable). This matters in the parity test that cross-validates Python and C++ outputs:

import math

for i, (py_val, cpp_val) in enumerate(zip(py_result, cpp_result)):
    if math.isnan(py_val):
        assert math.isnan(cpp_val), f"index {i}: Python=NaN but C++={cpp_val}"
    else:
        assert abs(py_val - cpp_val) < 1e-9, f"index {i}: Python={py_val}, C++={cpp_val}"

math.isnan vs numpy.isnan

FunctionWorks onReturnsUse when
math.isnan(x)A single Python floatboolPure Python path, no NumPy dependency
numpy.isnan(x)Scalars, arrays, Seriesbool or array of boolsNumPy/Pandas pipeline
x != xAny float-likeboolRarely — obscure, avoid in production code
x == float('nan')—Always FalseNever — this is a bug, not a NaN check
NaN propagation contract If the C++ extension outputs NaN at positions 0 through window-2 and a real value at position window-1 onward, the Python fallback must do exactly the same. If they differ — e.g. Python emits None or a different sentinel — downstream code that does math.isnan(result[i]) will crash or silently misbehave on the Python path only.

8. Dashboard UX: Surfacing Capability Flags with st.warning

The Streamlit dashboard at app/dashboard.py imports oil_volume.USING_CPP and shows a warning banner when the C++ extension is absent. The warning is shown in the results panel, where performance-sensitive computation happens — not in the sidebar or a footer where it could be missed.

app/dashboard.py — capability flag display
from oil_alpha.oil_volume import USING_CPP

if not USING_CPP:
    st.warning(
        "Running unoptimised: oil_volume_cpp extension not found. "
        "Metric kernels are using pure Python — results are correct "
        "but may be slower. Run `pip install -e .` to compile the extension."
    )

Why st.warning and not st.error or st.info

FunctionVisual treatmentSemantic meaningWhen to use
st.error()Red bannerSomething is broken; results may be wrongPipeline failure, data fetch error
st.warning()Yellow bannerDegraded mode; results are correct but limitedMissing optional component (C++ extension)
st.info()Blue bannerInformational; no action requiredExplaining a methodology choice
st.success()Green bannerPositive outcomeConfirming a completed action

st.warning is the right choice because the system is functional but not operating at full capability. Using st.error would be misleading — results are mathematically correct. Using st.info would under-communicate — the user might not realise they are on a slower path.

The warning message should include the remediation

A good capability warning tells the user three things: (1) what is degraded, (2) why it matters, and (3) how to fix it. "Run pip install -e . to compile the extension" is the remediation step. Without it, the user knows something is wrong but not what to do about it.

Show once, not per-render

Because USING_CPP is a module-level constant, the if not USING_CPP: check in the dashboard is evaluated every time Streamlit re-renders the page. That is fine — it is a cheap boolean read. But the visual placement matters: put the warning near the output it affects, not buried in a section the user scrolls past.

9. End-to-End Mental Model

At import time (once per Python session): import oil_alpha.oil_volume │ ▼ try: import oil_volume_cpp as _cpp │ ┌────┴────────────────────────────────┐ │ Found (.so present, ABI matches) │ Not found (missing, wrong ABI, etc.) │ │ │ USING_CPP = True │ USING_CPP = False │ _cpp = <module> │ _cpp = None └────┬────────────────────────────────┘ │ ▼ Module ready. Public API defined (rolling_mean, capacity_utilization, etc.) At call time (per function call): oil_volume.rolling_mean(values, 20) │ if USING_CPP? ┌────┴──────────────────────────────┐ _cpp.rolling_mean(values, 20) _py_rolling_mean(values, 20) (C++, fast) (pure Python, correct) └────────────────┬──────────────────┘ │ same list[float] result On the dashboard (at render time): from oil_alpha.oil_volume import USING_CPP if not USING_CPP: st.warning("Running unoptimised ...")
The invariant The public API of oil_volume.py is always correct regardless of which backend is active. The only thing that differs is speed. The USING_CPP flag communicates the capability state without leaking implementation details to callers.
Connection to Lesson 0001 This lesson builds directly on the pybind11 + CMake extension from Lesson 0001. Lesson 0001 explains how the oil_volume_cpp.so is built. This lesson explains what happens in production when that .so is absent — the fallback wrapper ensures the system stays operational.
